clue.text: Cabins Gladys fitted out with little money — they involved short commons?

definitions.note: plural noun phrase, matching the plural answer

indicators.note: fitting out a cabin rearranges what is in it, so the named letters are refitted in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
M is the abbreviation for money

explanation.surface: Gladys kits out some cabins on a shoestring budget, and the occupants go hungry.
explanation.walkthrough: SCAMBLING DAYS is an obsolete term for days in Lent when no regular meals were served and people scrambled for scraps; 'short commons' means meagre rations.
explanation.definitionFit: Scambling days were fasting days with makeshift meals, so they did indeed involve scanty rations, the old sense of short commons.

clue.text: One fires shot daily — see moving target caught

indicators.note: caught says the other pieces are trapped inside the daily paper

parts.note: the Sun is a British daily newspaper
see is the name of the letter C when spoken, so it stands for that letter

indicators.note: moving means shifting about, so the letters of target are rearranged

parts.note: the word target, taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone shoots at a moving target every day and hits it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'see' gives C, as the letter's name sounds; 'moving' shuffles TARGET to ATTERG; both are 'caught' in the Sun, a British daily tabloid.
explanation.definitionFit: A scattergun is a shotgun, a weapon that fires a spread of pellets, so it is one that fires shot.

clue.text: Like a crystal Archibald's sculpted — not bad

indicators.note: sculpted means carved into a new shape, so the name's letters are reworked
not says certain letters are left out of the rearranged name

parts.note: the name Archibald, with 's read as is

explanation.surface: Someone admires a crystal figure carved by Archibald and judges it decent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not bad' reads as faint praise for the sculpture, but it asks for B, A and D to be dropped from ARCHIBALD's letters before 'sculpted' rearranges what remains.
explanation.definitionFit: Chiral is a chemistry and crystallography term for a structure that is not superimposable on its mirror image, a property of some crystals.

clue.text: Island fast revealing hostility to poet

parts.note: Malta is a Mediterranean island
Lent is the Christian period of fasting

explanation.surface: An island's fasting season exposes some ill feeling towards a poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to poet' is Azed's way of saying the word belongs to a poet's vocabulary, here Spenser's; 'fast' looks like speed but is the religious fast.
explanation.definitionFit: Maltalent is a Spenserian word for ill will or malice, so it is hostility in the poet's usage.

clue.text: Cut danger inherent in wager

indicators.note: what is inherent in something lies within it, so one word sits inside the other

parts.note: a bet is a wager
risk is danger

explanation.surface: Any gamble carries some danger of loss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' could be a verb, but it is the butcher's noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Brisket is a cut of beef taken from the breast of the animal.

clue.text: Fool confined in cell unkindly

indicators.note: something confined in a space is held within it, so the letters sit inside the following words

parts.note: the letters run across the boundary of these two words

explanation.surface: A foolish prisoner is treated harshly in a cell.
explanation.definitionFit: Lunk, short for lunkhead, is an informal word for a stupid, clumsy person.

clue.text: Scots miserly — about right? Love it

indicators.note: 'about' means going round, so the word for love surrounds the abbreviation for right

parts.note: love is a zero score in tennis, i.e. nil
R is the abbreviation for right
taken as written

explanation.surface: A question about whether the Scots are tight-fisted, answered with a cheerful 'love it'.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces are assembled out of clue order; 'Love' is the tennis zero, disguised by the cheerful 'Love it'.
explanation.definitionFit: Nirlit is a Scots word meaning stunted or pinched, and by extension niggardly or stingy.

clue.text: Highlander set about opening of area

indicators.note: 'about' means surrounding, so the word for set goes round the selected letter

parts.note: to gel is to set, as a jelly does

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter, so only that letter is kept

parts.note: the first letter of area

explanation.surface: A Scotsman settles in around the edge of a region.
explanation.definitionFit: A Gael is a Gaelic-speaking Celt, typically someone from the Scottish Highlands.

clue.text: How drought affects region, always restricting clear lake

indicators.note: to restrict something is to hem it in, so the word for always encloses the rest

parts.note: ay (aye) is an old word for always, as in 'for ay'
to rid is to clear
L is the abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: A dry spell parches a region that is forever trying to keep its lake clear.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a whole phrase answered by an adverb: how does drought affect a region?
explanation.definitionFit: Drought makes land dry, so it affects a region in an arid manner; the answer is an adverb answering 'how'.

clue.text: What raja may accompany, always full of energy? Reverse of that

indicators.note: the reverse of the whole construction is wanted, so it is read backwards
a thing full of something holds it inside, so the word for always surrounds the energy word

parts.note: ay (aye) is an old word for always
go means energy or vigour

explanation.surface: A puzzle about what accompanies a lively raja, rounded off with a demand to turn it round.
explanation.walkthrough: Raja yoga is a classical form of Hindu yoga focused on meditation; 'that' refers to the whole construction just built.
explanation.definitionFit: In 'raja yoga' the word raja is followed by the answer, so the answer is what raja may accompany.

clue.text: Heads for Harwich after alert reports North Sea mist

indicators.note: the heads of words are their first letters, so only the initials are kept

parts.note: the first letters of these four words

explanation.surface: Ships bound for Harwich are warned of sea fog after an alert.
explanation.walkthrough: Harwich is a port on the Essex coast of the North Sea, which fits the picture neatly.
explanation.definitionFit: Haar is the cold sea fog that rolls in off the North Sea onto the east coasts of Scotland and England.

clue.text: Not bright about road, mistaken course

indicators.note: about says the dim word goes round the rearranged road

parts.note: dim means not bright

indicators.note: mistaken means wrong, so the letters of road are put in the wrong order

explanation.surface: A dull-witted driver goes the wrong way along a road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mistaken' shuffles ROAD to ADRO, and DIM goes 'about' it. This is a rare word from Chambers, as Azed answers often are.
explanation.definitionFit: Chambers gives diadrom as an obsolete word for a course or passage, as of a pendulum's swing or a vibration.

clue.text: Italian sausages made of minced meat or hollow inside

indicators.note: inside says the extra pieces are placed within the minced meat
minced means chopped finely, so the letters of meat and or are jumbled

parts.note: the words meat and or, taken as written
a dell is a small wooded hollow or valley

explanation.surface: A recipe note: Italian sausages are made of chopped meat or contain a hollow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'minced' turns MEAT OR into MORTAE, and DELL goes 'inside' it before the last E. The blog instead minces MEAT alone and puts OR and DELL inside it separately; the letters come out the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Mortadelle is the plural of mortadella, a large Italian pork sausage from Bologna.

clue.text: When imbibing I desist from vintage Scotch perhaps

definitions.note: 'Scotch' is a label: the Scots word for perhaps

indicators.note: to imbibe is to take in, so the word for when takes the other pieces inside

parts.note: as means when, as in 'as I left'
taken as written
blin is an old Spenserian word for to cease or desist

explanation.surface: Someone sipping wine wonders whether to give up the vintage, maybe for whisky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vintage' marks an archaic word, and 'Scotch' looks like whisky but labels the definition as Scots.
explanation.definitionFit: Aiblins (also ablins) is the Scots word for perhaps or possibly.

clue.text: Honeysuckle, if enveloped in top part

parts.note: a cap is a top or lid

indicators.note: something enveloped in a cover is wrapped inside it, so the little word goes inside the word for part

parts.note: a role is a part in a play
taken as written

explanation.surface: A honeysuckle wrapped round the top section of something, such as a trellis.
explanation.definitionFit: Caprifole is an old name for honeysuckle or woodbine, from the Latin for goat-leaf.

clue.text: Old woman in truth abandoning husband

indicators.note: to abandon someone is to leave them behind, so that letter is dropped

parts.note: troth is an old word for truth or good faith
H is the abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: An elderly woman, to tell the truth, has left her husband.
explanation.walkthrough: TROTH loses its H. 'Old woman' could look like a mother or wife, but here it is a single word for a hag.
explanation.definitionFit: Trot is an old contemptuous word for an old woman, a hag.

clue.text: Garrison commander a month after defeat

indicators.note: 'after' places the following pieces later, so the defeat word comes first

parts.note: to kill can mean to defeat, as a bill is killed
Adar is a month of the Jewish calendar

explanation.surface: A garrison's commanding officer is defeated, and a month passes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after' puts the month behind the defeat, reversing the clue's order.
explanation.definitionFit: A killadar is the commandant of a fort or garrison in India, from Persian.

clue.text: Food for Maoris? This mostly includes an aniseed liquor

indicators.note: to include something is to hold it within, so the shortened word surrounds the drink
mostly means not quite all, so the final letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: taken as written, then cut short
an is the indefinite article, A
raki is an aniseed-flavoured spirit from Turkey and the Balkans

explanation.surface: A question about Maori food, answered by a dish laced with an aniseed spirit.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a definition by example: this fish is one food Maoris eat.
explanation.definitionFit: The tarakihi is a New Zealand sea fish with a Maori name, a traditional catch and food.

clue.text: Last bit of lunch left for pet

indicators.note: the last bit of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the final letter of lunch
in cricket the on side is the leg side, which is on the left for a right-handed batsman

explanation.surface: The final scraps of lunch are left out for the family pet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' for ON is a stretch: the blog commenters suggested the cricket on side, the leg side, which is the batsman's left for a right-hander.
explanation.definitionFit: Hon, short for honey, is an informal term of endearment, as is pet.

clue.text: Part of chair back was in place at fringes of town library?

indicators.note: to sit at the fringes of something is to be on both its edges, so one word wraps round the other

parts.note: to sit is to be in place, past tense sat
PL is the abbreviation for public library, the kind a town has

explanation.surface: A chair at the edge of a town library broke apart, part of its back left in place.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark acknowledges that a town library is only one example of a public one.
explanation.definitionFit: A splat is the flat upright central piece of wood in the back of a chair.

clue.text: News mag distributed for Aussie itinerants?

indicators.note: distributing things scatters them about, so the letters are spread into a new order

parts.note: the letters of both words, taken together

explanation.surface: A news magazine circulated among travelling Australians.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark hints that the answer is mainly an Australian word.
explanation.definitionFit: Swagmen are tramps of the Australian outback who carried their belongings in a bundle, the swag.

clue.text: A dominant principle betraying discrimination of a kind

parts.note: taken as written
Geist is the German word for spirit, used of a guiding or dominant principle, as in zeitgeist

explanation.surface: A ruling ideology that reveals a certain kind of prejudice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'betraying' (revealing) belongs to the definition, showing that the answer is the adjective rather than the noun ageism.
explanation.definitionFit: Something ageist shows prejudice based on age, so it reveals one particular kind of bias.

clue.text: Parasite, any cut from local plants

indicators.note: what is cut from something is removed, so those letters come out of the longer word

parts.note: the botany of a region is its plant life
taken as written; these letters are removed

explanation.surface: A parasite, any one of them, is removed from the local vegetation.
explanation.walkthrough: BOTANY minus ANY. 'Botany' here means a region's flora as a whole, not the science.
explanation.definitionFit: A bot is the larva of the botfly, a parasite living in horses and other animals.

clue.text: Fall on bottom, end of cord coming away

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, which is the one to go

parts.note: the bed of a sea or river is its bottom

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fall on bottom' reads as one tumble, but 'Fall on' is the definition and 'bottom' starts the wordplay; ROPE loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Bedrop is an old word meaning to drop upon or sprinkle, so it means to fall on something.

clue.text: Rising celebrity breaking Nelson's heart? They were lovers

indicators.note: to break into something is to get inside it, so one piece is set within the other
the heart of a word is its middle, so only the central letters are kept

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means reading from bottom to top, so the word runs backwards

parts.note: a big name is a celebrity

explanation.walkthrough: Nelson and Emma Hamilton were famous lovers, which makes the surface apt.
explanation.definitionFit: Lemans is the plural of leman, an archaic word for a lover or sweetheart, often an illicit one.

clue.text: Treasury chap I found in heart of in-tray, looking back

indicators.note: looking back means facing the other way, so the result is read backwards
something found in another thing lies inside it
the heart of a word is its centre, so only the middle letters are kept

parts.note: the two middle letters of intray
the ego is the self, the I

explanation.walkthrough: 'Treasury' looks like the finance ministry, but it is a treasury of words, a thesaurus.

clue.text: Hospital dept. was poorly involved

parts.note: ENT is the ear, nose and throat department of a hospital
to ail is to be unwell

explanation.surface: A hospital department was itself in poor shape and got caught up in things.
explanation.definitionFit: To entail is to involve as a necessary consequence, so entailed means involved.

clue.text: Eggs arranged and put in grades as before

clue.text: West country watercourse at no time going the wrong way

clue.text: Spot providing environment for male duck

parts.note: to spot is to see

clue.text: Passionate person once displaying energy in pursuit of fabulous bird

clue.text: Bullets, number almost all explosive

parts.note: ammo, short for ammunition, covers bullets

taken as written, then cut short

clue.text: What bird enthusiast erects, best constructed during night classically (7, two words)

parts.note: nox is the Latin for night, and Nox the Roman goddess of night

clue.text: Drive former president out of party?

indicators.note: a do is a party, and out of says its two letters, the D and O at the ends of the name, are dropped

parts.note: Delano is the middle name of Franklin Delano Roosevelt, US president 1933 to 1945

clue.text: Businesswoman making opening that involves changing n rupees

indicators.note: that involves says the opening word takes the reworked letters inside it

parts.note: an entree is an entry or way in, an opening

parts.note: the word rupees, taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: 'opening' is a noun, an entry or way in, not the verb; the reworked letters of n and rupees go inside that word, before its final letter. Currency exchange fits the businesswoman.
explanation.definitionFit: An entrepreneuse is the feminine form of entrepreneur, a woman who sets up and runs businesses.
